rationale: This is the fourth sell-through variant in the archive and simply swaps the conditioning leg from the R&D level (already tested at t=4.68) to the previously tested R&D-deepening-per-employee leg, so the MIN is a recombination of two known legs whose likely driver remains the sell-through term rather than a new mechanism.

Both legs are already in the archive (Research Budget Deepening per Employee; R&D Gross-Profit Labor Leverage / R&D Labor-Productivity Spread) and both are scaled by employment, so the conditional overlap is partly mechanical (low-headcount firms rank high on both) rather than a distinct economic interaction.

The transmission framing — funding pressure that actually forces R&D cuts — is a substantively different conditioning variable from the archive's R&D-level liquidity signals, though it sits in tension with the archive's finding that R&D *increases* plus cash depletion also predicted negative returns, so the diagnostic value lies mainly in resolving that asymmetry.

This is the fourth gdwl/at × (X) composite on the same template, and multiplying an unranked bounded ratio by an unranked dollars-per-employee variable means the product's dispersion is dominated by the R&D term, so the "goodwill-conditioned" interpretation is not what the expression actually computes.

Replacing che with invt in the already-tested dlc/(dlc+che) × R&D-intensity design is a cosmetic denominator swap, and it is close to tautological because R&D-intensive firms mechanically hold little inventory, inflating the first leg for exactly the firms selected by the second.

Economically the denominator is incoherent — inventory plus a three-year R&D sum is not a meaningful capital base for gross profit — so the signal reduces largely to gross-profitability growth (a known anomaly) perturbed by a noisy scaler, and its closest archive predecessor (Dual-Capital Turnover Improvement) already produced zero alpha.
